newsitem.title: UK: British alcopop drinks to change their image.
newsitem.headline: British alcopop drinks to change their image.

text.p: Britain's new breed of "Alcopops", fruit-flavoured alcoholic drinks, are heading for a change of image after a drinks industry body on Wednesday upheld complaints that they targeted under-age drinkers.
A smiling fruit image used by brewing and drinks group Bass to market its "Hoopers Hooch" alcopop will be removed, while Whitbread will change the name of its "Lemon Jag" and "Vanilla Heist" brands.

The moves are in response to a report on complaints about the marketing of alcopops which was published on Wednesday by the Portman Group, a body funded by seven leading brewers and distillers to promote sensible drinking.

The market for alcopops is worth around 250 million pounds ($390 million) a year in Britain and growing fast. Bass has a market share of about 70 percent, while supermarkets have jumped on the bandwagon with own-label versions.
Alcohol concern groups say the new drinks target drinkers under the legal drinking age of 18 years.

The industry body said there were objections to Whitbread's "Heist" name because of associations with anti-social behaviour -- the name means a robbery -- while "Jag" has connections with the jargon of illegal drugs.
Neither Bass nor Whitbread will remove current stocks from sale but said the changes would be made once existing packaging was used up. They have not yet decided on replacements.

"Today's report shows that self-regulation is working. Drinks companies have show their commitment to the code comes before short-term brand considerations," Portman Group director Jean Coussins said in a statement.
Bass said there was no evidence to suggest that the images it used were attracting under-age drinkers but it accepted the opinion of the group.
The Portman Group said it had also persuaded Spilt Drinks to remove a cartoon character from its Jammin' brand of alcopop.

Carlsberg-Tetley, whose alcopops include Lemonhead and Orangehead, escaped criticism. But it described as premature a report in the Financial Times newspaper that it had decided not to sell its new Thickhead line in shops and off-licences.
"No final decision on any aspect of Thickhead marketing has yet been made," a spokesman said.
The Portman Group said Carlsberg-Tetley had agreed to re-label Thickhead last month, while the company said the label was within Portman Group guidelines.
The Portman Group, of which Bass and Whitbread are both founder members, said one in five complaints considered had been upheld and stressed its commitment to reducing alcohol misuse.
"If parents, doctors, teachers or anyone else is concerned about a drinks product or the way it is sold, the code enables them to bring a complaint to our attention," Coussins said.
Sixteen complaints that drinks targeted under-age drinking were thrown out, the Portman Group said. ($1=.6385 Pound)
